section_summary: This section covers State Department and Treasury Department documentation from late October 1941 to February 1944 regarding Japanese government officials, researchers, and commercial personnel in the United States immediately before and during World War II. The pre-Pearl Harbor materials focus on diplomatic requests, FBI surveillance reports, and statutory certifications under Section 116(h) of the Internal Revenue Code for income tax exemptions and sailing permits for Japanese nationals returning home on vessels such as the Tatuta Maru, Hikawa Maru, and Argentina. The section concludes with cross-reference sheets concerning detained officials and 1944 wartime correspondence between the Army's Civil Affairs Training School at the University of Chicago and the State Department regarding guest lectures and the background of former Japanese adviser Frederick Moore.

subfiles.about: The Acting Secretary of the Treasury confirms that income tax exemption instructions will be issued for Yaroku Katayama.
subfiles.from: Acting Secretary of the Treasury (John L. Sullivan)
subfiles.summary: The Acting Secretary of the Treasury acknowledges the Secretary of State's letter of November 4, 1941, concerning tax exemption for Yaroku Katayama. Katayama was in the United States on an official mission for the Japanese Government and scheduled to sail from Seattle on the Hikawa Maru. In view of the State Department's certification of reciprocity under Section 116(h) of the Internal Revenue Code, appropriate instructions were issued to Internal Revenue officials.
subfiles.title: Exemption from Federal Income Tax for Yaroku Katayama

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum discussing the Japanese Embassy's request for income tax exemption for Yaroku Katayama.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum details a request relayed by Miss Marsh of the Division of Foreign Service Administration from the Japanese Embassy regarding tax exemption for Yaroku Katayama, head of the New York branch of the Osaka Commercial Museum. It reviews administrative precedents under Section 116(h) of the Internal Revenue Code concerning foreign governmental employees, noting past exemptions for British personnel and Japanese commercial museum staff. The Division of Far Eastern Affairs concluded there was no objection to certifying Katayama for exemption prior to his departure from Seattle.
subfiles.title: Income Tax Exemption Request for Yaroku Katayama

subfiles.about: The Acting Secretary of the Treasury confirms that income tax exemption instructions have been issued for Kiyohiko Tsurumi and Ryozo Sunobe.
subfiles.from: Acting Secretary of the Treasury (John L. Sullivan)
subfiles.summary: The Treasury Department acknowledges the Secretary of State's letter of November 4, 1941, concerning income tax exemption for Kiyohiko Tsurumi and Ryozo Sunobe. Both were researchers for the Japanese Department of Foreign Affairs sent to the United States to study for the diplomatic service and were departing from Seattle on the Hikawa Maru. Based on the State Department's Section 116(h) certification of reciprocal treatment by Japan, instructions were issued to Internal Revenue officials.
subfiles.title: Exemption from Federal Income Tax for Kiyohiko Tsurumi and Ryozo Sunobe

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum relaying FBI intelligence regarding the departure of Taro Tokunaga and the movements of other Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: M. Flohr conveys information received by telephone from Mr. McLaughlin of the FBI to Mr. Warren. The FBI reported that Taro Tokunaga and his wife were departing on November 21 aboard the S.S. Excambion for Europe en route to Berlin via Switzerland to meet Kuroda of the Berlin Embassy. It also notes that Kuroda and New York Consul General Morito Morishima were in Washington and planned to return to New York that evening.
subfiles.title: FBI Report on Departures and Movements of Japanese Nationals

subfiles.about: The Acting Secretary of the Treasury confirms that income tax exemption instructions will be issued for Dr. Kiyoshi Hayakawa.
subfiles.from: Acting Secretary of the Treasury (John L. Sullivan)
subfiles.summary: The Acting Secretary of the Treasury replies to the Secretary of State's letter of November 27, 1941, concerning Dr. Kiyoshi Hayakawa. Hayakawa, a Japanese national who had been in the United States on an official mission, was preparing to sail from New York aboard the steamship Argentina. Relying on the State Department's reciprocity certification under Section 116(h) of the Internal Revenue Code, appropriate instructions were issued to Internal Revenue officials.
subfiles.title: Exemption from Federal Income Tax for Dr. Kiyoshi Hayakawa

subfiles.about: The Japanese Embassy requests tax exemptions and sailing permits for Yoshio Katagiri, Shokichi Mogami, and Yukio Suetsugu.
subfiles.summary: In Note No. 338, the Japanese Ambassador informs the Secretary of State of the scheduled departure of Yoshio Katagiri of the Japanese Financial Commission, and Shokichi Mogami and Yukio Suetsugu of the Raw Silk Bureau. The officials derived their income solely from the Japanese Government and were scheduled to sail from Los Angeles on December 16, 1941, on the Tatuta Maru. The Ambassador requests that their names be referred to appropriate authorities for tax exemption and issuance of sailing permits in Los Angeles (with a duplicate copy on pages 170-171).
subfiles.title: Note No. 338 from Japanese Embassy Requesting Tax Exemption for Katagiri, Mogami, and Suetsugu

subfiles.about: The Treasury Department confirms tax exemption instructions for four Japanese Foreign Office officials attached to the Japan Institute.
subfiles.from: Acting Secretary of the Treasury (John L. Sullivan)
subfiles.summary: The Acting Secretary of the Treasury acknowledges the State Department's letter of December 4, 1941, regarding Tamon Maeda, Isao Ashida, Toshiro Shimanouchi, and Shinzo Kaji. These Japanese Foreign Office officials assigned to the Japan Institute in New York were preparing to depart for Japan aboard the Tatuta Maru from Los Angeles on December 16. In accordance with the Section 116(h) reciprocity certification, instructions were issued to Internal Revenue officials to grant their exemptions and sailing documents in New York.
subfiles.title: Exemption from Federal Income Tax for Japan Institute Officials

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording the transmission of a list of Japanese subjects who departed from the United States.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Note No. 337 from the Japanese Embassy, dated December 3, 1941. The original paper transmitted a list of Japanese subjects who had departed from the United States. The document was filed under decimal file 811.111 Regis-Exemption/1652.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: List of Japanese Subjects Departed from U.S.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet referencing a report from the Coordinator of Information regarding Japanese agents under investigation in the United States.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference note records a confidential letter dated December 1, 1941, from Coordinator of Information William J. Donovan. The communication transmitted a list dated November 27, 1941, of past and/or present Japanese agents in the United States who were under active investigation. The original confidential paper was filed under 894.20210/126.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Japanese Agents in the United States

subfiles.about: The Japanese Embassy requests income tax exemption and a sailing permit for Professor Kiyoshi Hayakawa of Tokyo Imperial University.
subfiles.summary: Note No. 321 from the Japanese Ambassador informs the Secretary of State of the departure of Dr. Kiyoshi Hayakawa, a professor of Tokyo Imperial University residing in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Hayakawa had been sent to the United States by the Japanese Government for study, receiving his compensation exclusively from Japan. Having arrived in Honolulu in April 1941 aboard the Yawata Maru, he planned to sail from New York on November 24 aboard the steamship Argentina and requested his sailing permit in New York (with copies filed on pages 176 and 177).
subfiles.title: Note No. 321 from Japanese Embassy Requesting Tax Exemption for Dr. Kiyoshi Hayakawa

subfiles.about: The Secretary of State acknowledges the Japanese Embassy's request regarding tax exemption and sailing permit for Dr. Kiyoshi Hayakawa.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State acknowledges receipt of Japanese Embassy Note No. 321 of November 18, 1941, concerning Dr. Kiyoshi Hayakawa. The note states that the substance of the Ambassador's request was telephoned to the competent United States authorities with a view to exempting Hayakawa from Federal income tax on his official compensation. It notes his upcoming departure from New York on the steamship Argentina and his desire to obtain his sailing permit there.
subfiles.title: Note Acknowledging Request for Tax Exemption of Dr. Kiyoshi Hayakawa

subfiles.about: The Secretary of State certifies reciprocal income tax exemption under Section 116(h) of the Internal Revenue Code for Dr. Kiyoshi Hayakawa.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull writes to Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau, Jr., confirming telephone notification of November 19, 1941, regarding Dr. Kiyoshi Hayakawa. Hull certifies that the Japanese Government grants an equivalent tax exemption to American officials in Japan and that the services performed are similar. This formal certification under Section 116(h) of the Internal Revenue Code enabled Hayakawa's exemption from Federal income tax.
subfiles.title: Certification of Tax Exemption for Dr. Kiyoshi Hayakawa
subfiles.to: Secretary of the Treasury (Henry Morgenthau, Jr.)

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum summarizing FBI surveillance of Japanese bank officials departing on the Tatuta Maru and consular officials conferring in Washington.
subfiles.summary: M. Flohr reports information received from Mr. Laughlin of the FBI regarding movements of Japanese officials. Officials of the Yokohama Specie Bank (S. Yamada, Shoichiro Kashiwagi, T. Doida) and the Bank of Chosen (K. Hiraka, N. Andoh) were scheduled to sail for Japan on the Tatuta Maru from Los Angeles. Additionally, Japanese Consul K. Hirasawa was traveling from New York to Washington to confer with H. Terasaki and H. Takagi at the Japanese Embassy.
subfiles.title: FBI Report on Movements of Japanese Bankers and Consular Officials

subfiles.about: The Japanese Embassy requests income tax exemptions and sailing permits for four Foreign Office officials attached to the Japan Institute.
subfiles.summary: In Note No. 325, the Japanese Ambassador informs the Secretary of State of the planned departure of Tamon Maeda, Isao Ashida, Toshiro Shimanouchi, and Shinzo Kaji, all Foreign Office officials attached to the Japan Institute in New York. The note details their roles, arrival dates, and local addresses, confirming their compensation was derived solely from Japan. They planned to leave New York before December 7 to board the Tatuta Maru sailing from Los Angeles on December 16, requesting tax exemptions and expedited sailing permits (with a duplicate of page 1 filed on page 183).
subfiles.title: Note No. 325 from Japanese Embassy Requesting Tax Exemption for Japan Institute Officials

subfiles.about: The Secretary of State provides Section 116(h) certification of income tax exemption for four officials of the Japan Institute.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull writes to Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau, Jr., confirming telephone notification of December 1, 1941, regarding Tamon Maeda, Isao Ashida, Toshiro Shimanouchi, and Shinzo Kaji of the Japan Institute. Hull certifies under Section 116(h) of the Internal Revenue Code that reciprocal tax exemptions are granted by the Japanese Government to American officials in Japan. This enabled the four officials to obtain their sailing documents in New York prior to sailing from Los Angeles on the Tatuta Maru.
subfiles.title: Certification of Tax Exemption for Officials of the Japan Institute
subfiles.to: Secretary of the Treasury (Henry Morgenthau, Jr.)

subfiles.about: The Secretary of State acknowledges the Japanese Embassy's request regarding tax exemption and departure arrangements for Japan Institute officials.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State acknowledges receipt of Note No. 325 of November 29, 1941, from the Japanese Ambassador regarding Tamon Maeda, Isao Ashida, Toshiro Shimanouchi, and Shinzo Kaji. The note confirms that their desire to obtain sailing documents in New York before departing on the Tatuta Maru from Los Angeles was communicated to competent authorities. It assures the Ambassador that steps were taken to exempt the officials from Federal income tax on their official compensation.
subfiles.title: Note Acknowledging Request for Tax Exemption of Japan Institute Officials

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording the transmission to the Department of Justice of a list of Japanese independent office employees.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet records the transmission to the Justice Department of a list of Japanese nationals notified to the State Department as officials or employees of independent offices of the Japanese Government. It notes that while the Department understood some individuals had departed, no official notice of departure had been received from the Japanese Embassy. The original paper was filed under 701.9411/1632a.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: List of Japanese Officials and Employees Transmitted to Justice Department

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet referencing a consular telegram from Casablanca reporting on Tamon Maeda.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Telegram No. 114 sent from Casablanca at 10 p.m. on April 4, 1942. The telegram contains a report on Tamon Maeda, describing him as probably the parent of the newly appointed Japanese Consul. The original telegram was filed under decimal file 702.9481/10.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Report on Tamon Maeda

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet regarding a Japanese Embassy communication requesting the reciprocal release of detained Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference note records a communication dated December 10, 1941, from the Japanese Embassy concerning Japanese Government officials detained in the United States following the outbreak of war. The note requested their release on condition of reciprocity for American officials in Japan. The original document was filed under decimal file 701.9411/1744.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Release of Detained Japanese Government Officials

subfiles.about: Captain Cecil G. Tilton inquires about Frederick Moore's background and invites State Department officials to lecture at the Civil Affairs Training School.
subfiles.summary: Captain Cecil G. Tilton of the Army's Civil Affairs Training School at the University of Chicago writes to Joseph W. Ballantine of the State Department. Tilton asks for advice on whether former adviser Frederick Moore should be invited to lecture specialist sections, invites Ballantine to spend a full day lecturing on Japanese government procedure, and asks whether Edward S. Benninghoff would be available to speak on Manchoukuo.
subfiles.title: Letter from Captain Cecil G. Tilton to Joseph W. Ballantine Regarding Civil Affairs Training Lectures

subfiles.about: Joseph W. Ballantine assesses Frederick Moore's loyalty and confirms lecturer availability for the Civil Affairs Training School.
subfiles.summary: Joseph W. Ballantine replies to Captain Cecil G. Tilton regarding Frederick Moore, stating that Moore's past service for the Japanese Embassy appeared above-board and consistent with loyalty as an American citizen, though some might feel skeptical of his former ties. Ballantine regrets being unable to travel to Chicago immediately due to official business in Washington, but confirms that Edward S. Benninghoff is available to lecture on Manchoukuo and suggests Tilton contact him directly.
subfiles.title: Letter from Joseph W. Ballantine to Captain Cecil G. Tilton Regarding Frederick Moore and Lectures
